vector spaces: A linear map $T : V \to W$ is \textbf{injective} if and only if $\ker T = \{0\}$.
A linear map $T : V \to W$ is \textbf{surjective} if and only if $\operatorname{im} T = W$.
The \textbf{rank} of a linear map $T : V \to W$ is $\dim \operatorname{im} T$.
For subspaces $U, W \subseteq V$, $\dim(U + W) = \dim U + \dim W - \dim(U \cap W)$.
A list of vectors $(v_1, \dots, v_k)$ in $V$ is \textbf{linearly independent} if $\sum_i \lambda_i v_i = 0$ implies $\lambda_i = 0$ for all $i$.
Every linearly independent subset of a finite-dimensional vector space extends to a basis.
Every spanning set of a finite-dimensional vector space contains a basis.
For finite-dimensional $V$, every subspace $W \subseteq V$ satisfies $\dim W \leq \dim V$, with equality iff $W = V$.
The \textbf{external direct sum} $U \oplus W$ of two vector spaces is the Cartesian product $U \times W$ with componentwise operations.
For vector spaces $V, W$ over $F$, $\operatorname{Hom}_F(V, W)$ is itself a vector space over $F$ under pointwise addition and scalar multiplication.
If $V$ is finite-dimensional and $W \subseteq V$ is a subspace, then $\dim(V/W) = \dim V - \dim W$.
A linear map $T : V \to V$ is \textbf{diagonalizable} if $V$ has a basis consisting of eigenvectors of $T$.
A scalar $\lambda \in F$ is an \textbf{eigenvalue} of $T : V \to V$ if there exists a nonzero $v \in V$ with $T(v) = \lambda v$; such $v$ is an \textbf{eigenvector}.
For finite-dimensional $V$ and $T : V \to V$, $T$ is invertible if and only if $\ker T = \{0\}$.
The \textbf{annihilator} of a subset $S \subseteq V$ in $V^*$ is $S^0 = \{f \in V^* : f(s) = 0 \text{ for all } s \in S\}$, a subspace of $V^*$.
For finite-dimensional $V$ and a subspace $W$, $\dim W^\circ + \dim W = \dim V$.
Two linear maps $S, T : V \to W$ are equal if and only if they agree on every element of some basis of $V$.

The \textbf{change-of-basis matrix} from basis $\mathcal{B}$ to basis $\mathcal{B}'$ of $V$ is the invertible matrix whose columns are the coordinates of the $\mathcal{B}$-vectors expressed in $\mathcal{B}'$.
For linear maps $T : V \to W$ and a subspace $U \subseteq V$, the restriction $T|_U : U \to W$ is linear.

The \textbf{trace} of an endomorphism $T : V \to V$ on a finite-dimensional space is $\operatorname{tr}(T) = \sum_i f_i(T(e_i))$ for any basis $(e_i)$ with dual basis $(f_i)$, independent of the choice of basis.
For finite-dimensional $V$, the natural isomorphism $V \cong V^{**}$ identifies each $v \in V$ with the evaluation functional $\hat{v} : f \mapsto f(v)$ on $V^*$.
The \textbf{transpose} of $T : V \to W$ is the linear map $T^* : W^* \to V^*$ defined by $T^*(g) = g \circ T$.
For linear $T : V \to W$, $\ker T^* = (\operatorname{im} T)^\circ$ and $\operatorname{im} T^* = (\ker T)^\circ$ when $V, W$ are finite-dimensional.
A \textbf{flag} in $V$ is a strictly increasing chain of subspaces $\{0\} = V_0 \subsetneq V_1 \subsetneq \cdots \subsetneq V_k = V$.
The \textbf{symmetric square} $\operatorname{Sym}^2(V)$ is the quotient of $V \otimes_F V$ by the subspace spanned by elements $v \otimes w - w \otimes v$.
The \textbf{exterior square} $\bigwedge^2 V$ is the quotient of $V \otimes_F V$ by the subspace spanned by elements $v \otimes v$.
For a finite-dimensional inner product space over $\mathbb{R}$, every subspace $W$ satisfies $V = W \oplus W^\perp$, where $W^\perp = \{v \in V : \langle v, w \rangle = 0 \text{ for all } w \in W\}$.
The \textbf{minimal polynomial} of $T : V \to V$ on a finite-dimensional $V$ is the monic polynomial of least degree $p \in F[x]$ with $p(T) = 0$.
Two endomorphisms $S, T \in \operatorname{End}_F(V)$ are \textbf{similar} if there exists an invertible $P \in \operatorname{End}_F(V)$ with $S = P T P^{-1}$.
A bilinear form $B : V \times V \to F$ is \textbf{nondegenerate} if $B(v, w) = 0$ for all $w \in V$ implies $v = 0$.
module theory: Assume $R$ is a field. An $R$-module homomorphism $\varphi : M \to N$ is \textbf{injective} if and only if $\varphi^{-1}(0) = \{0\}$.
Assume $R$ is a field. An $R$-module homomorphism $\varphi : M \to N$ is \textbf{surjective} if and only if $\varphi(M) = N$.
Assume $R$ is a field. The \textbf{rank} of a homomorphism $\varphi : M \to N$ between free $R$-modules of finite rank is $\operatorname{rank}_R \varphi(M)$.
Assume $R$ is a field. For $R$-submodules $A, B \subseteq M$, $\operatorname{rank}_R(A + B) = \operatorname{rank}_R A + \operatorname{rank}_R B - \operatorname{rank}_R(A \cap B)$.
Assume $R$ is a field. A finite list $(m_1, \dots, m_k)$ in $M$ is \textbf{$R$-linearly independent} if $\sum_i r_i m_i = 0$ with $r_i \in R$ implies each $r_i = 0$.
Assume $R$ is a field. Every $R$-linearly independent subset of a finitely generated $R$-module extends to a free generating set.
Assume $R$ is a field. Every generating set of a finitely generated $R$-module contains a free generating set.
Assume $R$ is a field. For a free $R$-module $M$ of finite rank and an $R$-submodule $N$, $\operatorname{rank}_R N \leq \operatorname{rank}_R M$, with equality if and only if $N = M$.
Assume $R$ is a field. The \textbf{external direct sum} $M \oplus N$ of two $R$-modules is the Cartesian product $M \times N$ with componentwise $R$-action.
Assume $R$ is a field. $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M, N)$ is an $R$-module under pointwise addition $(\varphi + \psi)(m) = \varphi(m) + \psi(m)$ and scalar action $(r\varphi)(m) = r\varphi(m)$.
Assume $R$ is a field. For a free $R$-module $M$ of finite rank $n$ and a submodule $N$, $M/N$ is free of rank $n - \operatorname{rank}_R N$.
Assume $R$ is a field. An endomorphism $\varphi \in \operatorname{End}_R(M)$ is \textbf{diagonalizable} if $M$ has a free generating set consisting of eigenvectors of $\varphi$.

Assume $R$ is a field. An element $r \in R$ is an \textbf{eigenvalue} of $\varphi \in \operatorname{End}_R(M)$ if there exists a nonzero $m \in M$ with $\varphi(m) = rm$; such $m$ is called an \textbf{eigenvector}.
Assume $R$ is a field. For a finitely generated $R$-module $M$ and $\varphi \in \operatorname{End}_R(M)$, $\varphi$ is invertible if and only if $\varphi^{-1}(0) = \{0\}$.

Assume $R$ is a field. The \textbf{annihilator} of a subset $S \subseteq M$ is $\operatorname{Ann}(S) = \{\psi \in \operatorname{Hom}_R(M, R) : \psi(s) = 0 \text{ for all } s \in S\}$, an $R$-submodule of $\operatorname{Hom}_R(M, R)$.
Assume $R$ is a field. For a free $R$-module $M$ of finite rank and a submodule $N$, $\operatorname{rank}_R \operatorname{Ann}(N) + \operatorname{rank}_R N = \operatorname{rank}_R M$.
Assume $R$ is a field. Two $R$-module homomorphisms $\varphi, \psi : M \to N$ are equal if and only if they agree on every element of any free generating set of $M$.

Assume $R$ is a field. For a free $R$-module $M$ with free generating sets $\mathcal{B}$ and $\mathcal{B}'$, the \textbf{change-of-basis matrix} is the invertible element of $\operatorname{End}_R(R^n)$ expressing the $\mathcal{B}$-generators in terms of $\mathcal{B}'$.
Assume $R$ is a field. For $\varphi : M \to N$ and a submodule $L \subseteq M$, the restriction $\varphi|_L : L \to N$ is an $R$-module homomorphism.

Assume $R$ is a field. For a free $R$-module $M$ of finite rank with free generators $(x_1, \dots, x_n)$ and dual generators $(\xi_i)$, $\operatorname{tr}(\varphi) = \sum_i \xi_i(\varphi(x_i))$ is independent of the choice of free generators.

Assume $R$ is a field. For a finitely generated free $R$-module $M$, the evaluation map $M \to \operatorname{Hom}_R(\operatorname{Hom}_R(M, R), R)$ sending $m$ to the evaluation-at-$m$ functional is a natural isomorphism of $R$-modules.

Assume $R$ is a field. The \textbf{transpose} of $\varphi : M \to N$ is the $R$-module homomorphism $\varphi^\top : \operatorname{Hom}_R(N, R) \to \operatorname{Hom}_R(M, R)$ defined by $\varphi^\top(g) = g \circ \varphi$.

Assume $R$ is a field. For $\varphi : M \to N$ between finitely generated free $R$-modules, $\varphi^{-1}(0)$ and the annihilator of $\varphi(M)$ have equal rank, and similarly for $\varphi(M)$ and the annihilator of $\varphi^{-1}(0)$.
Assume $R$ is a field. A \textbf{filtration} of an $R$-module $M$ is a chain of submodules $0 = M_0 \subseteq M_1 \subseteq \cdots \subseteq M_k = M$.
Assume $R$ is a field. The \textbf{symmetric square} $\operatorname{Sym}^2_R(M)$ is the quotient of $M \otimes_R M$ by the submodule generated by elements $m \otimes m' - m' \otimes m$.
Assume $R$ is a field. The \textbf{exterior square} $\bigwedge^2_R M$ is the quotient of $M \otimes_R M$ by the submodule generated by elements of the form $m \otimes m$.

Assume $R$ is a field. For a free $R$-module $M$ equipped with a nondegenerate symmetric $R$-bilinear form $\beta$, there exists an orthogonal decomposition $M = N \oplus N^\perp$ for every free direct summand $N \subseteq M$.

Assume $R$ is a field. The \textbf{minimal polynomial} of $\varphi \in \operatorname{End}_R(M)$ for finitely generated free $M$ is the monic polynomial of least degree $p \in R[x]$ such that $p(\varphi) = 0$.

Assume $R$ is a field. Two endomorphisms $\varphi, \psi \in \operatorname{End}_R(M)$ are \textbf{similar} if there exists an invertible $\alpha \in \operatorname{End}_R(M)$ with $\varphi = \alpha \circ \psi \circ \alpha^{-1}$.

Assume $R$ is a field. An $R$-balanced pairing $\beta : M \times N \to R$ is \textbf{nondegenerate} if $\beta(m, n) = 0$ for all $n \in N$ implies $m = 0$, and $\beta(m, n) = 0$ for all $m \in M$ implies $n = 0$.
probability: A sequence of random variables $\{X_n\}$ is uniformly integrable if $\sup_n \mathbb{E}[|X_n| \mathbf{1}_{|X_n| > M}] \to 0$ as $M \to \infty$.
The moment generating function of $X$ is $M_X(t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{tX}]$, defined for all $t$ in a neighborhood of zero when it exists finitely.
For random variables $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ that are independent and identically distributed with finite mean $\mu$, $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^n X_k \to \mu$ almost surely.
If $X_1, X_2, \ldots$ are i.i.d. with mean $0$ and variance $\sigma^2 < \infty$, then $\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}}\sum_{k=1}^n X_k \to \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2)$ in distribution.
The covariance of square-integrable random variables $X$ and $Y$ is $\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y) = \mathbb{E}[(X - \mathbb{E}[X])(Y - \mathbb{E}[Y])] = \mathbb{E}[XY] - \mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]$.
A filtration on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P)$ is an increasing family $(\mathcal{F}_t)_{t \geq 0}$ of sub-$\sigma$-algebras of $\mathcal{F}$.
A process $(M_n, \mathcal{F}_n)_{n \geq 0}$ is a martingale if each $M_n$ is integrable, $\mathcal{F}_n$-measurable, and $\mathbb{E}[M_{n+1} \mid \mathcal{F}_n] = M_n$ almost surely.
For a martingale $(M_n)$ bounded in $L^1$, the limit $M_\infty = \lim_{n \to \infty} M_n$ exists almost surely.
A stopping time $\tau$ with respect to $(\mathcal{F}_n)$ is a random variable taking values in $\{0,1,2,\ldots\} \cup \{\infty\}$ such that $\{\tau \leq n\} \in \mathcal{F}_n$ for all $n$.
For an integrable martingale $(M_n)$ and bounded stopping time $\tau$, $\mathbb{E}[M_\tau] = \mathbb{E}[M_0]$.
The conditional expectation operator $X \mapsto \mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]$ is a contraction on $L^p$ for each $p \geq 1$: $\|\mathbb{E}[X \mid \mathcal{G}]\|_p \leq \|X\|_p$.
Two events $A$ and $B$ are conditionally independent given $\mathcal{G}$ if $P(A \cap B \mid \mathcal{G}) = P(A \mid \mathcal{G}) P(B \mid \mathcal{G})$ almost surely.
A probability measure $Q$ is absolutely continuous with respect to $P$ on $(\Omega, \mathcal{F})$ if $P(A) = 0$ implies $Q(A) = 0$ for every $A \in \mathcal{F}$.
If $Q \ll P$, there exists a nonnegative $\mathcal{F}$-measurable random variable $Z$ with $\mathbb{E}_P[Z] = 1$ such that $Q(A) = \mathbb{E}_P[Z \mathbf{1}_A]$ for all $A \in \mathcal{F}$.
The entropy of a discrete random variable $X$ taking values in a countable set is $H(X) = -\sum_x P(X = x) \log P(X = x)$.
For random variables $X$ and $Y$, $\mathrm{Var}(X + Y) = \mathrm{Var}(X) + \mathrm{Var}(Y) + 2\,\mathrm{Cov}(X, Y)$.
If $X$ and $Y$ are independent, then for all measurable $A$ and $B$, $P(X \in A \mid Y \in B) = P(X \in A)$ whenever $P(Y \in B) > 0$.

The joint characteristic function of $(X, Y)$ is $\varphi_{X,Y}(s, t) = \mathbb{E}[e^{i(sX + tY)}]$; $X$ and $Y$ are independent iff $\varphi_{X,Y}(s,t) = \varphi_X(s)\varphi_Y(t)$ for all $s, t \in \mathbb{R}$.
For a random variable $X \geq 0$ with $p > 0$, $\mathbb{E}[X^p] = p \int_0^\infty t^{p-1} P(X > t)\, dt$.
A sequence of distribution functions $F_n$ converges weakly to $F$ iff $F_n(t) \to F(t)$ at every continuity point $t$ of $F$.
The $k$-th cumulant $\kappa_k$ of a random variable $X$ is the coefficient of $(it)^k / k!$ in the cumulant generating function $\log \varphi_X(t)$.
A random vector $(X_1, \ldots, X_n)$ is exchangeable if its joint distribution is invariant under all permutations of the indices.
A Gaussian random variable $X \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ has characteristic function $\varphi_X(t) = \exp(i\mu t - \tfrac{1}{2}\sigma^2 t^2)$.
For a Poisson random variable $X$ with parameter $\lambda > 0$, $P(X = k) = e^{-\lambda} \lambda^k / k!$ for $k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots$, and $\mathbb{E}[X] = \mathrm{Var}(X) = \lambda$.
A random variable $X$ is symmetric about zero iff $X$ and $-X$ have the same distribution.

The tail $\sigma$-algebra of a sequence $(X_n)$ is $\mathcal{T} = \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty \sigma(X_n, X_{n+1}, \ldots)$; by Kolmogorov's zero-one law, every event in $\mathcal{T}$ has probability zero or one when the $X_n$ are independent.
For $p \geq 1$ and a random variable $X$, $\|X\|_p = (\mathbb{E}[|X|^p])^{1/p}$; the triangle inequality $\|X + Y\|_p \leq \|X\|_p + \|Y\|_p$ holds for all $X, Y \in L^p$.
If $1 \leq p \leq q < \infty$ and $\mu(\Omega) = 1$, then $\mathbb{E}[|X|^p]^{1/p} \leq \mathbb{E}[|X|^q]^{1/q}$, i.e., $L^q \subseteq L^p$ on probability spaces.
The $\sigma$-algebra generated by a random variable $X$ is $\sigma(X) = \{X^{-1}(B) : B \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R})\}$, and $Y$ is $\sigma(X)$-measurable iff $Y = h(X)$ for some Borel function $h$.
The Borel–Cantelli lemma in the converse direction states: if $(A_n)$ are pairwise independent and $\sum_n P(A_n) = \infty$, then $P(A_n \text{ i.o.}) = 1$.
measure theory: A family of measurable functions $\{f_\alpha\} \subset L^1(\mu)$ is uniformly integrable if $\sup_\alpha \int_{\{|f_\alpha| > M\}} |f_\alpha|\, d\mu \to 0$ as $M \to \infty$.
The Laplace transform of a nonnegative measurable function $f$ with respect to $\mu$ is $\mathcal{L}_f(s) = \int_X e^{-sf}\, d\mu$, defined for $s \geq 0$.

For $\sigma$-finite measure spaces $(X, \Sigma, \mu)$ and a sequence of nonneg­ative measurable $f_n$ with $f_n \to f$ $\mu$-a.e., if $\int f_n\, d\mu \to \int f\, d\mu < \infty$ then $\int |f_n - f|\, d\mu \to 0$.
For $f_n \to f$ in measure and $|f_n| \leq g \in L^1(\mu)$, one has $\int f_n\, d\mu \to \int f\, d\mu$.
For $f \in L^p(\mu)$ and $g \in L^q(\mu)$ with $1 < p < \infty$ and $1/p + 1/q = 1$, equality holds in $\int |fg|\, d\mu \leq \|f\|_p \|g\|_q$ iff $|f|^p$ and $|g|^q$ are proportional $\mu$-a.e.

A measure $\mu$ on a topological space $(X, \tau)$ is inner regular if $\mu(E) = \sup\{\mu(K) : K \subseteq E,\, K \text{ compact}\}$ for every Borel set $E$.
A measure $\mu$ on a locally compact Hausdorff space is a Radon measure if it is locally finite and inner regular on Borel sets.

For $1 \leq p < \infty$, the dual of $L^p(\mu)$ is isometrically isomorphic to $L^q(\mu)$ where $1/p + 1/q = 1$, via the pairing $\langle f, g \rangle = \int fg\, d\mu$.
For $f \in L^1_{\mathrm{loc}}(\mathbb{R}^d, \lambda)$, the Hardy–Littlewood maximal function is $Mf(x) = \sup_{r > 0} \frac{1}{\lambda(B_r(x))} \int_{B_r(x)} |f|\, d\lambda$.
A measurable function $f : (X, \Sigma, \mu) \to \mathbb{R}$ is essentially bounded if there exists $M < \infty$ with $\mu(\{|f| > M\}) = 0$; the infimum of such $M$ is $\|f\|_{L^\infty(\mu)}$.
For $p = \infty$ and $q = 1$, Hölder's inequality reads $\int |fg|\, d\mu \leq \|f\|_{L^\infty(\mu)} \|g\|_{L^1(\mu)}$.
The $L^p$ norm satisfies the interpolation inequality $\|f\|_r \leq \|f\|_p^\theta \|f\|_q^{1-\theta}$ whenever $1/r = \theta/p + (1-\theta)/q$ and $0 < \theta < 1$.
A sequence $(f_n)$ in $L^2(\mu)$ converges weakly to $f$ iff $\int f_n g\, d\mu \to \int fg\, d\mu$ for every $g \in L^2(\mu)$.
For a finite measure $\mu$ on $(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d))$, the convolution $\mu * \nu$ is the pushforward of $\mu \otimes \nu$ under the addition map $(x,y) \mapsto x + y$.
The essential supremum $\mathrm{ess\,sup}_\mu f = \inf\{M : \mu(\{f > M\}) = 0\}$ is the smallest $M$ that bounds $f$ $\mu$-almost everywhere.
A measurable map $T : (X, \Sigma, \mu) \to (X, \Sigma, \mu)$ is measure-preserving if $\mu(T^{-1}(E)) = \mu(E)$ for all $E \in \Sigma$.
A measure-preserving transformation $T$ is ergodic if every $T$-invariant set $E$ (i.e., $T^{-1}(E) = E$) satisfies $\mu(E) \in \{0, 1\}$.
For an ergodic measure-preserving $T$ on a probability space and $f \in L^1(\mu)$, $\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=0}^{n-1} f \circ T^k \to \int f\, d\mu$ $\mu$-a.e. and in $L^1$.
On a $\sigma$-finite measure space, two $L^2$ functions satisfy $\|f + g\|_2^2 = \|f\|_2^2 + \|g\|_2^2$ iff $\int fg\, d\mu = 0$.

A collection $\mathcal{A} \subset 2^X$ is a $\pi$-system if it is closed under finite intersections; the $\sigma$-algebra it generates is characterized by the fact that any two measures agreeing on $\mathcal{A}$ agree on $\sigma(\mathcal{A})$, provided the total masses agree.

The tail $\sigma$-algebra of a sequence of measurable functions $(f_n)$ is $\mathcal{T} = \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty \sigma(f_n, f_{n+1}, \ldots)$; on a normalized space with independent $(f_n)$, every $E \in \mathcal{T}$ satisfies $\mu(E) \in \{0,1\}$.

For a sub-$\sigma$-algebra $\mathcal{T} \subset \Sigma$ and $f \in L^p(\mu)$ with $p \geq 1$, the conditional expectation satisfies $\|\mathbb{E}^\mu[f \mid \mathcal{T}]\|_{L^p(\mu)} \leq \|f\|_{L^p(\mu)}$.

For a locally compact abelian group $G$ with Haar measure $\lambda$, the Fourier transform of $f \in L^1(\lambda)$ is $\hat{f}(\xi) = \int_G f(x) e^{-i\xi(x)}\, d\lambda(x)$, and the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma states $\hat{f}(\xi) \to 0$ as $\xi \to \infty$.
set theory: For sets $A$ and $B$, $A \cap B = \{x : x \in A \text{ and } x \in B\}$.
For sets $A$ and $B$, $A \cup B = \{x : x \in A \text{ or } x \in B\}$.
For sets $A$ and $B$, $A \setminus B = \{x \in A : x \notin B\}$.
The symmetric difference $A \triangle B = (A \setminus B) \cup (B \setminus A)$.
For a set $A$, $|\mathcal{P}(A)| = 2^{|A|}$.
Cantor's theorem: for any set $A$, there is no surjection $A \twoheadrightarrow \mathcal{P}(A)$.
A function $f : A \to B$ has a left inverse iff $f$ is injective.
A function $f : A \to B$ has a right inverse iff $f$ is surjective (assuming the axiom of choice).
The axiom of choice: for every family $\{A_i\}_{i \in I}$ of nonempty sets, $\prod_{i \in I} A_i \neq \emptyset$.
An ordinal $\alpha$ is a transitive set well-ordered by $\in$.
The von Neumann ordinals: $0 = \emptyset$, $n+1 = n \cup \{n\}$, and $\omega = \{0, 1, 2, \ldots\}$.
A cardinal $\kappa$ is an ordinal not in bijection with any smaller ordinal.
The Cantor–Bernstein theorem: if there exist injections $A \hookrightarrow B$ and $B \hookrightarrow A$, then $|A| = |B|$.
For cardinals $\kappa$ and $\lambda$, $\kappa + \lambda = |\kappa \sqcup \lambda|$ and $\kappa \cdot \lambda = |\kappa \times \lambda|$.
For sets $A$ and $B$ with $|B| = \kappa$, $|B^A| = \kappa^{|A|}$.
A set $A$ is finite iff it is in bijection with some $n \in \omega$.
A set $A$ is countably infinite iff $|A| = |\omega| = \aleph_0$.
Zermelo's well-ordering theorem: every set can be well-ordered (equivalent to the axiom of choice).
The axiom of regularity: every nonempty set $A$ contains an element $x$ with $x \cap A = \emptyset$.
For sets $A \subseteq B$, the inclusion $\iota : A \hookrightarrow B$ is the function $\iota(a) = a$.
A relation $R \subseteq A \times A$ is a partial order if it is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive.
A relation $R \subseteq A \times A$ is a well-order if it is a total order and every nonempty subset of $A$ has an $R$-least element.
For $f : A \to B$, the fiber over $b \in B$ is $f^{-1}(\{b\}) = \{a \in A : f(a) = b\}$.
The transitive closure of a set $A$ is $\mathrm{TC}(A) = A \cup \bigcup A \cup \bigcup\bigcup A \cup \cdots$.
For ordinals $\alpha < \beta$, $\alpha \in \beta$; in particular, $\alpha = \{\gamma : \gamma < \alpha\}$.
The axiom of union: for any set $A$, $\bigcup A = \{x : \exists B \in A,\ x \in B\}$ is a set.
The axiom of pairing: for any $a, b$, the set $\{a, b\}$ exists.
The replacement axiom: for any set $A$ and definable function $F$, $\{F(a) : a \in A\}$ is a set.
Two functions $f, g : A \to B$ are equal iff $f(a) = g(a)$ for all $a \in A$.
A set $A$ is Dedekind-infinite iff there exists an injection $A \hookrightarrow A$ that is not a surjection.
category theory: A functor $F : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{D}$ assigns to each object $A$ an object $FA$ and to each arrow $f : A \to B$ an arrow $Ff : FA \to FB$, preserving identities and composition.

A natural transformation $\eta : F \Rightarrow G$ between functors $F, G : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{D}$ assigns to each object $A$ an arrow $\eta_A : FA \to GA$ such that $\eta_B \circ Ff = Gf \circ \eta_A$ for all $f : A \to B$.
A natural isomorphism $\eta : F \Rightarrow G$ is a natural transformation in which every component $\eta_A$ is an isomorphism.

An adjunction $F \dashv G$ between $F : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{D}$ and $G : \mathbf{D} \to \mathbf{C}$ is a natural bijection $\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{D}}(FA, B) \cong \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(A, GB)$.
The unit of an adjunction $F \dashv G$ is a natural transformation $\eta : \mathrm{Id}_{\mathbf{C}} \Rightarrow G \circ F$.
The counit of an adjunction $F \dashv G$ is a natural transformation $\varepsilon : F \circ G \Rightarrow \mathrm{Id}_{\mathbf{D}}$.

A monad on $\mathbf{C}$ is a triple $(T, \eta, \mu)$ where $T : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{C}$ is a functor, $\eta : \mathrm{Id} \Rightarrow T$, and $\mu : T^2 \Rightarrow T$, satisfying $\mu \circ T\eta = \mu \circ \eta T = \mathrm{id}_T$ and $\mu \circ T\mu = \mu \circ \mu T$.

A comonad on $\mathbf{C}$ is a triple $(W, \varepsilon, \delta)$ where $W : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{C}$, $\varepsilon : W \Rightarrow \mathrm{Id}$, and $\delta : W \Rightarrow W^2$, satisfying the dual monad axioms.
The Yoneda lemma: for a functor $F : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$ and an object $A$, there is a natural bijection $\mathrm{Nat}(\mathrm{Hom}(A, -), F) \cong FA$.
An object $A$ is a representable functor if $F \cong \mathrm{Hom}(A, -)$ for some functor $F : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{Set}$.
The limit of a diagram $D : \mathbf{J} \to \mathbf{C}$ is a universal cone $(L, \{\lambda_j\}_{j \in \mathbf{J}})$ with $\lambda_j : L \to Dj$.
The colimit of a diagram $D : \mathbf{J} \to \mathbf{C}$ is a universal cocone $(L, \{\iota_j\}_{j \in \mathbf{J}})$ with $\iota_j : Dj \to L$.
A functor $F : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{D}$ is full if for every $A, B \in \mathbf{C}$, the map $\mathrm{Hom}(A, B) \to \mathrm{Hom}(FA, FB)$ is surjective.
A functor $F : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{D}$ is faithful if for every $A, B \in \mathbf{C}$, the map $\mathrm{Hom}(A, B) \to \mathrm{Hom}(FA, FB)$ is injective.

An equivalence of categories consists of functors $F : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{D}$ and $G : \mathbf{D} \to \mathbf{C}$ with natural isomorphisms $GF \cong \mathrm{Id}_{\mathbf{C}}$ and $FG \cong \mathrm{Id}_{\mathbf{D}}$.
A functor $F : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{D}$ is an equivalence iff it is full, faithful, and essentially surjective.
Right adjoints preserve limits: if $G : \mathbf{D} \to \mathbf{C}$ is a right adjoint and $D : \mathbf{J} \to \mathbf{D}$ has a limit, then $G(\lim D) \cong \lim(G \circ D)$.
Left adjoints preserve colimits: if $F : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{D}$ is a left adjoint and $D : \mathbf{J} \to \mathbf{C}$ has a colimit, then $F(\mathrm{colim}\, D) \cong \mathrm{colim}(F \circ D)$.
The category $\mathbf{Set}$ is cartesian closed: for any sets $A, B, C$, there is a natural bijection $\mathrm{Hom}(A \times B, C) \cong \mathrm{Hom}(A, C^B)$.
The free monoid functor $F : \mathbf{Set} \to \mathbf{Mon}$ is left adjoint to the forgetful functor $U : \mathbf{Mon} \to \mathbf{Set}$.
The powerset functor $\mathcal{P} : \mathbf{Set} \to \mathbf{Set}$ carries a monad structure with unit $\eta_A(a) = \{a\}$ and multiplication $\mu_A(\mathcal{S}) = \bigcup \mathcal{S}$.
An Eilenberg–Moore algebra for a monad $(T, \eta, \mu)$ is a pair $(A, h : TA \to A)$ satisfying $h \circ \eta_A = \mathrm{id}_A$ and $h \circ \mu_A = h \circ Th$.
The Kleisli category of a monad $(T, \eta, \mu)$ on $\mathbf{C}$ has the same objects as $\mathbf{C}$ and morphisms $A \to B$ given by arrows $A \to TB$ in $\mathbf{C}$, composed via $\mu$.
A reflective subcategory $\mathbf{D} \hookrightarrow \mathbf{C}$ is one for which the inclusion functor has a left adjoint (the reflector).
An arrow $f : A \to B$ in $\mathbf{Set}$ is a monomorphism iff it is injective, i.e., $f \circ g = f \circ h$ implies $g = h$.
An arrow $f : A \to B$ in $\mathbf{Set}$ is an epimorphism iff it is surjective, i.e., $g \circ f = h \circ f$ implies $g = h$.
The diagonal functor $\Delta : \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{C}^{\mathbf{J}}$ sends each object $A$ to the constant diagram at $A$; limits and colimits are its right and left adjoints.
A slice category $\mathbf{C}/A$ has objects $(B, f : B \to A)$ and morphisms $h : (B, f) \to (B', f')$ satisfying $f' \circ h = f$.
The comma category $(F \downarrow G)$ for $F : \mathbf{A} \to \mathbf{C}$ and $G : \mathbf{B} \to \mathbf{C}$ has objects $(A, B, f : FA \to GB)$ and morphisms commuting squares.
In $\mathbf{Set}$, the copower $n \cdot A = \coprod_{i=1}^{n} A$ represents $\mathrm{Hom}(n \cdot A, B) \cong \mathrm{Hom}(A, B)^n$ naturally in $A$ and $B$.
geometry: A projective variety $X \subseteq \mathbb{P}^n_k$ is the common vanishing locus of a homogeneous ideal in $k[x_0, \ldots, x_n]$.
A morphism of varieties $f: X 	o Y$ is an isomorphism iff it admits a two-sided inverse morphism $g: Y 	o X$.
The fiber of a morphism $f: V 	o W$ over a point $q \in W$ is the closed subvariety $f^{-1}(q) \subseteq V$.
A rational map $V \dashrightarrow W$ between irreducible varieties is an equivalence class of morphisms defined on dense open subsets.
A dominant morphism $f: V 	o W$ of irreducible varieties is one whose image is Zariski dense in $W$.
The intersection multiplicity of two plane curves $C_1, C_2 \subseteq \mathbb{A}^2$ at a point $p$ is the dimension of the local ring $\mathcal{O}_{p} / (f_1, f_2)$ as a $k$-vector space.
A Cartier divisor on a variety $V$ is a global section of the sheaf of Weil divisors modulo principal divisors.
The tangent cone to $V$ at a singular point $p$ is the variety defined by the lowest-degree homogeneous part of the defining equations of $V$ translated to $p$.
A blow-up of a variety $V$ at a closed subvariety $Z$ replaces $Z$ with the projectivized normal cone $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}_{Z/V})$.
A birational morphism $f: V 	o W$ induces an isomorphism of function fields $k(V) \cong k(W)$.
The Picard group $\mathrm{Pic}(V)$ of a smooth variety $V$ is the group of line bundles on $V$ under tensor product.
A normal variety $V$ is one in which the local ring at every point is an integrally closed domain.
The degree of a hypersurface $H \subseteq \mathbb{P}^n$ is the degree of any homogeneous polynomial cutting it out.
Two varieties $V$ and $W$ are birationally equivalent iff they contain isomorphic open dense subvarieties.
A linear system on a variety $V$ is a projective space of effective Cartier divisors linearly equivalent to a fixed divisor $D$.
An ample divisor $D$ on a projective variety $V$ is one such that some positive multiple $mD$ embeds $V$ into projective space.
A smooth morphism $f: X 	o Y$ of varieties is one whose relative tangent sheaf is locally free of the expected rank.
The degree of a finite morphism $f: V 	o W$ of irreducible varieties is the degree of the field extension $[k(V): k(W)]$.
An affine variety $V$ is normal iff every rational function on $V$ that is integral over $k[V]$ is itself regular.
The exceptional divisor of a blow-up of $V$ along $Z$ is the preimage of $Z$, isomorphic to $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{N}_{Z/V})$.
A closed embedding $i: Z \hookrightarrow V$ is a morphism identifying $Z$ homeomorphically with a closed subvariety and inducing a surjection on sheaves of regular functions.
The Weil divisor class group of a normal variety $V$ is the group of codimension-one cycles modulo rational equivalence.
A morphism $f: V 	o W$ is étale at $p \in V$ iff the induced map on Zariski tangent spaces $T_p V 	o T_{f(p)} W$ is an isomorphism.
A variety $V$ is factorial iff every Weil divisor on $V$ is principal.
The graph of a morphism $f: V 	o W$ is the closed subvariety $\Gamma_f = \{(v, f(v))\} \subseteq V 	imes W$.
A projective morphism $f: V 	o W$ factors through a closed embedding $V \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^n_W$ for some $n$.
The singular locus of a variety $V$ is the closed subvariety of points at which $V$ is not smooth.
A complete variety $V$ over $k$ is one such that the projection $V 	imes W 	o W$ is a closed map for every variety $W$.
An affine variety $V$ is smooth of dimension $d$ iff $\Omega_{k[V]/k}$ is a projective $k[V]$-module of rank $d$.
The pull-back of a Cartier divisor $D$ on $W$ along a morphism $f: V 	o W$ is the Cartier divisor $f^*D$ on $V$ defined locally by composing the defining equation with $f$.
commutative algebra: A prime ideal $\mathfrak{p} \subset A$ is a proper ideal such that $A/\mathfrak{p}$ is an integral domain.
The nilradical of a ring $A$ is the intersection of all prime ideals of $A$, equivalently the set of all nilpotent elements.
A ring $A$ is reduced iff its nilradical is zero, i.e., it has no nonzero nilpotent elements.

The localization $S^{-1}A$ of a ring $A$ at a multiplicative set $S$ is the ring of fractions $a/s$ with $a \in A$, $s \in S$, under the equivalence $(a,s) \sim (b,t)$ iff $u(at-bs)=0$ for some $u \in S$.
An integral extension $A \subseteq B$ is one in which every element of $B$ satisfies a monic polynomial with coefficients in $A$.

The going-up theorem: if $A \subseteq B$ is an integral extension and $\mathfrak{p} \subseteq \mathfrak{q}$ are primes of $A$, then any prime $\mathfrak{P}$ of $B$ over $\mathfrak{p}$ extends to a prime $\mathfrak{Q}$ over $\mathfrak{q}$ with $\mathfrak{P} \subseteq \mathfrak{Q}$.
The integral closure of a domain $A$ in its fraction field is a normal domain containing $A$.
A Noetherian ring $A$ is one in which every ideal is finitely generated, equivalently every ascending chain of ideals stabilizes.
The spectrum $\operatorname{Spec}(A)$ of a commutative ring $A$ is the set of prime ideals of $A$ equipped with the Zariski topology.
A finitely generated module $M$ over a Noetherian ring $A$ is Noetherian, i.e., every submodule of $M$ is finitely generated.
Nakayama's Lemma: if $M$ is a finitely generated $A$-module and $\mathfrak{m}$ is the Jacobson radical of $A$, then $\mathfrak{m}M = M$ implies $M = 0$.
The tensor product $M \otimes_A N$ of $A$-modules $M$ and $N$ is the $A$-module representing bilinear maps out of $M 	imes N$.
A flat $A$-module $M$ is one for which the functor $M \otimes_A -$ is exact.
The depth of a module $M$ over a local ring $(A, \mathfrak{m})$ is the length of a maximal regular sequence on $M$ contained in $\mathfrak{m}$.
A Cohen–Macaulay ring $A$ is a Noetherian local ring in which $\operatorname{depth}(A) = \dim(A)$.
The associated primes of an $A$-module $M$ are the prime ideals $\mathfrak{p}$ such that $\mathfrak{p} = \operatorname{Ann}_A(m)$ for some $m \in M$.
A primary decomposition of an ideal $I \subseteq A$ is an expression $I = Q_1 \cap \cdots \cap Q_r$ where each $Q_i$ is primary.

An ideal $Q \subseteq A$ is primary iff $A/Q 
eq 0$ and every zero divisor in $A/Q$ is nilpotent.

The dimension formula for finitely generated algebras over a field: if $A$ is a finitely generated integral $k$-algebra and $\mathfrak{p} \subsetneq \mathfrak{q}$ are primes of $A$, then $\operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak{q}) = \operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak{p}) + \operatorname{ht}(\mathfrak{q}/\mathfrak{p})$.
A discrete valuation ring is a Noetherian local domain of Krull dimension one whose maximal ideal is principal.
The module of Kähler differentials $\Omega_{B/A}$ is the $B$-module generated by symbols $db$ for $b \in B$ subject to the Leibniz rule $d(b_1 b_2) = b_1\, db_2 + b_2\, db_1$.
The Hilbert basis theorem: if $A$ is a Noetherian ring then the polynomial ring $A[x]$ is also Noetherian.
For a finitely generated $k$-algebra $A$, the Krull dimension of $A$ equals the transcendence degree of $\operatorname{Frac}(A/\mathfrak{p})$ over $k$ for any minimal prime $\mathfrak{p}$.
A regular local ring $(A, \mathfrak{m}, k)$ is a Noetherian local ring satisfying $\dim_k(\mathfrak{m}/\mathfrak{m}^2) = \dim A$.
The completion $\hat{A}$ of a local ring $(A, \mathfrak{m})$ is $\varprojlim_n A/\mathfrak{m}^n$, equipped with the $\mathfrak{m}$-adic topology.
For a multiplicative set $S \subset A$ and an ideal $I \subseteq A$, the extension $S^{-1}I = \{a/s : a \in I, s \in S\}$ is an ideal in $S^{-1}A$.
A projective module $P$ over a ring $A$ is a direct summand of a free $A$-module.
The Jacobson radical of $A$ is the intersection of all maximal ideals of $A$.
A graded ring $A =  igoplus_{d \geq 0} A_d$ is a ring decomposed as a direct sum of abelian groups with $A_d \cdot A_e \subseteq A_{d+e}$.
For a Noetherian ring $A$ and an ideal $I \subseteq A$, the $I$-adic completion map $A 	o \hat{A}$ is flat.
topology: Every simply connected covering of $X$ is a universal cover, and any two universal covers of $X$ are isomorphic as covering spaces.
The long exact sequence of a fibration $F \hookrightarrow E 	woheadrightarrow B$ yields $\cdots \to \pi_1(F) \to \pi_1(E) \to \pi_1(B) \to \pi_0(F) \to \cdots$.
A covering map $p : Y \to X$ is a local homeomorphism such that every point of $X$ has an evenly covered open neighborhood.
The fundamental group of the Klein bottle is $\langle a, b \mid abab^{-1} = 1 \rangle$, a non-abelian group of cohomological dimension 2.
If $X$ is a CW complex with 0-skeleton and 1-skeleton $X^1$, then $\pi_1(X^1)$ surjects onto $\pi_1(X)$ with kernel normally generated by attaching maps of 2-cells.
A null-homotopic loop in $X$ lifts to a loop in any covering space $Y$, regardless of the choice of basepoint lift.
For a path-connected, locally path-connected, semi-locally simply connected space $X$, the universal covering space $\tilde{X}$ exists and is unique up to isomorphism.
The inclusion $S^1 \hookrightarrow D^2$ as boundary induces the zero map on $\pi_1$ since $D^2$ is contractible.
A retraction $r : X \to A$ of a subspace $A \hookrightarrow X$ induces a surjection $r_* : \pi_1(X) \twoheadrightarrow \pi_1(A)$ split by the inclusion-induced map.
Homotopy equivalences induce isomorphisms on all homotopy groups $\pi_n$ for $n \geq 0$.
The mapping cylinder of $f : X \to Y$ deformation retracts onto $Y$, so $\pi_1(\mathrm{Cyl}(f)) \cong \pi_1(Y)$.
A based map $f : X \to Y$ between $K(G,1)$ and $K(H,1)$ spaces is determined up to based homotopy by the induced homomorphism $f_* : G \to H$.
The fundamental group of a graph $\Gamma$ with $V$ vertices, $E$ edges, and $k$ connected components is the free group of rank $E - V + k$.
For a covering $p : Y \to X$ of degree $n < \infty$ and $[X]$ a triangulation, $Y$ admits a triangulation with $n$ times as many simplices.
The Seifert--van Kampen theorem applies to CW complexes by decomposing along subcomplexes, yielding amalgamated products over shared attaching regions.
For any normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq \pi_1(X, x_0)$, there exists a regular covering $p : Y \to X$ with deck transformation group isomorphic to $\pi_1(X)/N$.
The suspension $\Sigma X$ of a path-connected space $X$ is simply connected.
A deformation retraction $X \to A$ is a homotopy equivalence, so $\pi_1(X, a) \cong \pi_1(A, a)$ for any $a \in A$.
Any two paths in a simply connected space with the same endpoints are homotopic relative to their endpoints.
For the projective plane $\mathbb{RP}^2$, $\pi_1(\mathbb{RP}^2) \cong \mathbb{Z}/2$, realized as the non-trivial double cover $S^2 \to \mathbb{RP}^2$.
The $n$-fold cyclic cover of $S^1$ corresponding to the subgroup $n\mathbb{Z} \leq \mathbb{Z}$ is the map $z \mapsto z^n : S^1 \to S^1$.
If $f, g : X \to Y$ are homotopic maps, then $f_*$ and $g_*$ are conjugate as homomorphisms $\pi_1(X) \to \pi_1(Y)$.
The free homotopy classes of loops in $X$ are in bijection with conjugacy classes of elements of $\pi_1(X, x_0)$.
For a properly discontinuous free action of a group $G$ on a simply connected space $\tilde{X}$, the orbit space $\tilde{X}/G$ has fundamental group $G$.
A covering transformation (deck transformation) of $p : Y \to X$ is a homeomorphism $\phi : Y \to Y$ satisfying $p \circ \phi = p$.
The Hopf fibration $S^3 \to S^2$ has fiber $S^1$; the long exact sequence of homotopy groups gives $\pi_2(S^2) \cong \mathbb{Z}$ and $\pi_1(S^3) = 0$.
The fundamental group of the complement of a trefoil knot in $S^3$ is $\langle a, b \mid a^2 = b^3 \rangle$.
A covering map $p : Y \to X$ is a Serre fibration with discrete fibers, and path-lifting holds uniquely for all paths.
The Whitehead theorem states that a map between simply connected CW complexes inducing isomorphisms on all homology groups is a homotopy equivalence.
For a locally trivial fiber bundle $F \hookrightarrow E \to B$ with $B$ and $F$ path-connected, there is an exact sequence $\pi_1(F) \to \pi_1(E) \to \pi_1(B) \to \pi_0(F)$.
algebra: The abelianization of the free group $F_n$ is $\mathbb{Z}^n$, reflecting that first homology is the maximal abelian quotient of the fundamental group.
For a group $G$, the commutator subgroup $[G,G]$ is the kernel of the canonical surjection $G \twoheadrightarrow G^{\mathrm{ab}}$ onto the abelianization.

The normal closure of a subset $R \subseteq F(S)$ is the smallest normal subgroup of $F(S)$ containing $R$, equal to $\langle\langle R \rangle\rangle = \bigcap \{N \trianglelefteq F(S) : R \subseteq N\}$.
A group $G$ is free if and only if it acts freely on a tree (Bass-Serre theory).

The amalgamated free product $G_1 *_H G_2$ satisfies the universal property: for any group $K$ and homomorphisms $\varphi_i : G_i \to K$ agreeing on $H$, there is a unique $\varphi : G_1 *_H G_2 \to K$.
An HNN extension $G *_\phi = \langle G, t \mid t^{-1}at = \phi(a),\, a \in A \rangle$ adjoins a stable letter conjugating from a subgroup $A$ to a subgroup $B$ via an isomorphism $\phi : A \to B$.
A group $G$ is abelian if and only if the commutator map $[\cdot, \cdot] : G \times G \to G$ is identically the identity element.
Every quotient of a free group is a group presentation; conversely, every group arises as such a quotient.
The index $[G : H]$ of a subgroup $H$ in $G$ equals the number of left cosets of $H$, which equals the number of right cosets.
For a normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq G$, the short exact sequence $1 \to N \to G \to G/N \to 1$ splits if and only if $G$ is a semidirect product $N \rtimes G/N$.
The group of deck transformations of the covering corresponding to $H \leq G = \pi_1(X)$ is isomorphic to $N_G(H)/H$, where $N_G(H)$ is the normalizer of $H$ in $G$.
A group $G$ acts freely on a set $S$ if and only if every non-identity element of $G$ has no fixed points in $S$.
The kernel of a group homomorphism $\varphi : G \to H$ is a normal subgroup of $G$, and $\varphi$ induces an injection $G/\ker\varphi \hookrightarrow H$.
Two subgroups $H, K \leq G$ give conjugate $G$-actions on $G/H$ and $G/K$ if and only if $H$ and $K$ are conjugate in $G$.
A group $G$ is finitely presented if there exists a presentation $\langle S \mid R \rangle$ with both $S$ and $R$ finite sets.
The outer automorphism group of the free group $F_n$ for $n \geq 3$ is the mapping class group of the rose, acting on conjugacy classes of elements.
For groups $G_1, G_2$ with a common subgroup $H$, the Mayer-Vietoris sequence in homology relates $H_*(G_1 *_H G_2)$ to $H_*(G_1)$, $H_*(G_2)$, and $H_*(H)$.
A surjective group homomorphism $\varphi : G \twoheadrightarrow Q$ with kernel $N$ makes $G$ an extension of $Q$ by $N$; the set of equivalence classes is classified by $H^2(Q; N)$.
The center $Z(G)$ of a group $G$ is the set of elements commuting with all of $G$; $G/Z(G) \cong \mathrm{Inn}(G)$.
A free group on a set $S$ is characterized by the universal property: any function $S \to G$ into a group $G$ extends uniquely to a group homomorphism $F(S) \to G$.

The fundamental theorem of finitely generated abelian groups: every such group is isomorphic to $\mathbb{Z}^r \oplus \mathbb{Z}/d_1 \oplus \cdots \oplus \mathbb{Z}/d_k$ with $d_1 \mid d_2 \mid \cdots \mid d_k$.
For a transitive $G$-set $S$ and any $s \in S$, the stabilizer $G_s$ satisfies $G_s^{gs} = g G_s g^{-1}$, so stabilizers of different points are conjugate.
An action of $G$ on $\tilde{X}$ by deck transformations is properly discontinuous iff every point has a neighborhood meeting its $G$-translates only finitely often.

The torsion subgroup of $\mathbb{Z}^n$ is trivial; hence every finite-order element of $\pi_1(T^n)$ is trivial, so $T^n$ has no non-trivial finite-sheeted regular covers with abelian deck groups of finite order.
A group extension $1 \to N \to G \to Q \to 1$ is central if $N \subseteq Z(G)$; central extensions of $Q$ by $N$ are classified by $H^2(Q; N)$ with trivial $Q$-action.
For an exact sequence $1 \to H \to G \to K \to 1$ with $H$ and $K$ finite, $|G| = |H| \cdot |K|$ by the orbit-stabilizer theorem applied to coset multiplication.
A $G$-equivariant map between transitive $G$-sets $G/H$ and $G/K$ exists if and only if $H$ is conjugate to a subgroup of $K$.
The trefoil knot group $\langle a, b \mid a^2 = b^3 \rangle$ is isomorphic to the braid group $B_3$, and is not abelian but has abelianization $\mathbb{Z}$.
A group $G$ is perfect (i.e., $G = [G,G]$) if and only if $G^{\mathrm{ab}} = 0$, equivalently, $H_1(G;\mathbb{Z}) = 0$.
For a group $G$ of cohomological dimension at most 1, $G$ is free; this is the algebraic content of the Nielsen-Schreier theorem applied via projective resolutions.
graph theory: A graph $G$ is a tree iff it is connected and has exactly $|V(G)| - 1$ edges.
A perfect matching in $G$ is a set $M \subseteq E$ such that every vertex of $G$ is incident to exactly one edge of $M$.
The chromatic number $\chi(G)$ is the minimum number of colors needed to color the vertices of $G$ so that no two adjacent vertices share a color.
The clique number $\omega(G)$ is the size of the largest complete subgraph of $G$.
The independence number $\alpha(G)$ is the maximum size of a set $S \subseteq V$ with no two vertices of $S$ adjacent.
The girth of $G$ is the length of the shortest cycle in $G$.
A graph $G$ is Eulerian iff it is connected and every vertex has even degree.
A graph $G$ is Hamiltonian iff it contains a cycle passing through every vertex exactly once.
The vertex connectivity $\kappa(G)$ is the minimum number of vertices whose removal disconnects $G$ or leaves a single vertex.
The edge connectivity $\lambda(G)$ is the minimum number of edges whose removal disconnects $G$.
By Menger's theorem, the maximum number of internally vertex-disjoint paths between $s$ and $t$ equals the minimum vertex cut separating $s$ from $t$.
A graph $G$ is planar iff it can be drawn in the plane with no edge crossings.
By Euler's formula, for a connected planar graph, $|V| - |E| + |F| = 2$, where $F$ is the set of faces.
The line graph $L(G)$ has vertex set $E(G)$, with two vertices adjacent iff the corresponding edges share an endpoint in $G$.
A $k$-edge-coloring of $G$ is a coloring of edges with $k$ colors so that no two edges sharing a vertex receive the same color.
The Petersen graph is the unique $3$-regular graph on $10$ vertices with girth $5$.
A spanning tree of $G$ is a tree subgraph that includes every vertex of $G$.
A bridge of $G$ is an edge $e$ such that $G - e$ has more connected components than $G$.
A cut vertex of $G$ is a vertex $v$ such that $G - v$ has more connected components than $G$.
Two graphs $G$ and $H$ are cospectral if their adjacency matrices have the same multiset of eigenvalues yet $G \not\cong H$.
The eccentricity of a vertex $v$ in a connected graph $G$ is $\max_{u \in V} d(v, u)$; the radius of $G$ is $\min_v \operatorname{ecc}(v)$.
A dominating set $D \subseteq V$ satisfies the condition that every vertex in $V \setminus D$ has at least one neighbor in $D$.
The Turán number $\mathrm{ex}(n, H)$ is the maximum number of edges in an $n$-vertex graph containing no subgraph isomorphic to $H$.
A $k$-factor of $G$ is a $k$-regular spanning subgraph of $G$.
A graph $G$ is vertex-transitive if for every pair $u, v \in V$ there exists an automorphism mapping $u$ to $v$.

The strong product $G \boxtimes H$ has vertex set $V(G) \times V(H)$, with $(u,v)$ adjacent to $(u',v')$ iff $\max(|u - u'|, |v - v'|)$-type adjacency holds: $u = u'$ or $uu' \in E(G)$, and $v = v'$ or $vv' \in E(H)$, but not both equalities simultaneously.
A graph $G$ is $k$-connected iff $|V(G)| > k$ and no set of fewer than $k$ vertices separates $G$.
The Ramsey number $R(s,t)$ is the minimum $n$ such that every red-blue coloring of the edges of $K_n$ contains a red $K_s$ or a blue $K_t$.
A topological sort of a directed acyclic graph $G$ is a linear ordering of the vertices such that for every directed edge $uv$, $u$ appears before $v$.
The feedback vertex set of $G$ is a minimum set $S \subseteq V$ such that $G - S$ is acyclic.
linear algebra: The characteristic polynomial of $A$ is $p_A(\lambda) = \det(\lambda I - A)$; its roots are the eigenvalues of $A$.
The rank of the adjacency matrix $A(G)$ equals $n$ minus the dimension of its null space; for bipartite $G$ the rank is always even.
The algebraic connectivity (Fiedler value) $\mu_2 > 0$ iff $G$ is connected, where $0 = \mu_1 \leq \mu_2 \leq \cdots \leq \mu_n$ are the eigenvalues of $L$.
The Fiedler vector (eigenvector for $\mu_2$) can be used to partition $V$ into two sets achieving a near-minimum edge cut.
For a $d$-regular graph, the normalized adjacency matrix $\frac{1}{d}A$ has eigenvalues in $[-1, 1]$ with largest eigenvalue exactly $1$.
The spectral gap $d - \lambda_2(A)$ controls the rate of convergence of the simple random walk to its stationary distribution.
The number of closed walks of length $k$ is $\operatorname{tr}(A^k) = \sum_{i=1}^n \lambda_i^k$, where $\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_n$ are the eigenvalues of $A$.

The signless Laplacian $Q = D + A$ has eigenvalues $
u_1 \geq \cdots \geq 
u_n \geq 0$; $
u_n = 0$ iff $G$ has a bipartite component.
The normalized Laplacian $\mathcal{L} = D^{-1/2} L D^{-1/2}$ has eigenvalues in $[0, 2]$, with $2$ an eigenvalue iff $G$ has a bipartite component.
By the matrix-tree theorem, the number of spanning trees equals any cofactor of $L$, or equivalently $\frac{1}{n}\prod_{i=2}^{n}\mu_i$.
The adjacency matrix of $K_{m,n}$ has eigenvalues $\sqrt{mn}$, $-\sqrt{mn}$, and $0$ with multiplicity $m + n - 2$.
The Perron–Frobenius theorem guarantees that the largest eigenvalue $\lambda_1$ of $A$ (for connected $G$) is simple and has a strictly positive eigenvector.
For a $d$-regular graph, $\lambda_1(A) = d$ and $\|A - \frac{d}{n}J\|_2 = \lambda_2(A)$, which measures pseudorandomness.

Schur's lemma: any $G$-equivariant linear map between irreducible representations is either zero or an isomorphism; over $\mathbb{C}$, any equivariant endomorphism of an irreducible is a scalar.
For a finite abelian group $G$, every irreducible complex representation is one-dimensional, and $|\hat G| = |G|$.
The regular representation of a finite group $G$ decomposes as $\bigoplus_{\pi \in \hat G} \pi^{\oplus \dim \pi}$, giving $|G| = \sum_{\pi} (\dim \pi)^2$.
For compact $G$, the Peter–Weyl theorem states $L^2(G) \cong \widehat{\bigoplus}_{\pi \in \hat G} \mathrm{End}(V_\pi)$ as $G \times G$-representations.
The Frobenius reciprocity theorem states $\langle \mathrm{Ind}_H^G \sigma,\, \pi \rangle_G = \langle \sigma,\, \mathrm{Res}_H^G \pi \rangle_H$ for finite groups $H \leq G$.
For a locally compact abelian group $G$, the Fourier transform intertwines the convolution algebra $L^1(G)$ with $C_0(\hat G)$ via the Gelfand transform.
The dual of a finite cyclic group $\mathbb{Z}/n$ is again $\mathbb{Z}/n$, and Pontryagin duality exchanges the generator with the fundamental character $k \mapsto e^{2\pi i k/n}$.
For a compact abelian group $G$, the characters $\{\chi\}_{\chi \in \hat G}$ form a complete orthonormal system in $L^2(G)$ with respect to normalized Haar measure.
The Mackey criterion for irreducibility of $\mathrm{Ind}_H^G \sigma$ states that $\sigma$ must be distinct from all its nontrivial $G$-conjugates when restricted to $H$.
For a normal subgroup $N \trianglelefteq G$, the irreducible representations of $G/N$ lift to exactly those irreducible representations of $G$ whose restriction to $N$ is trivial.
On a locally compact abelian group, multiplication by a character $\chi_0$ in the spatial domain corresponds to translation by $\chi_0$ in $\hat G$.
The Plancherel formula for a finite group $G$ states $f(e) = \sum_{\pi \in \hat G} \dim(\pi)\, \mathrm{tr}(\hat f(\pi))$ for $f \in L^1(G)$.
A representation $\pi$ of $G$ is irreducible iff $\langle \chi_\pi, \chi_\pi \rangle = 1$, where the inner product is the normalized sum over $G$.
For a locally compact group $G$, the left regular representation on $L^2(G)$ is unitarily equivalent to its right regular representation iff $G$ is unimodular.
The annihilator of a subgroup $H \leq G$ in $\hat G$ is $H^\perp = \{\chi \in \hat G : \chi(h) = 1\ \forall h \in H\}$, and $|H^\perp| = |G|/|H|$ when $G$ is finite.
For a representation $\pi$ of a finite group $G$, $\dim \mathrm{Hom}_G(V,V) = \sum_\rho m_\rho^2$ where $m_\rho$ are the multiplicities of irreducibles $\rho$ in $V$.

The Mackey decomposition of $\mathrm{Res}_H^G \mathrm{Ind}_K^G \sigma$ is given by a double-coset formula indexed by $H \backslash G / K$.

For a finite group $G$, the character table is a square matrix whose rows and columns are mutually orthogonal, up to appropriate normalization.
The irreducible representations of a product group $G \times H$ are exactly $\{\pi \boxtimes \rho : \pi \in \hat G,\, \rho \in \hat H\}$, where $\pi \boxtimes \rho$ acts on $V_\pi \otimes V_\rho$.
For a locally compact abelian group $G$, the map $\hat G \to \mathrm{Spec}(L^1(G))$ given by $\chi \mapsto (f \mapsto \hat f(\chi))$ is a homeomorphism.

The Hopf algebra structure on $\Lambda$ has coproduct $\Delta(h_n) = \sum_{k=0}^n h_k \otimes h_{n-k}$ and antipode $S(h_n) = (-1)^n e_n$.

For $\lambda = (\lambda_1 \geq \lambda_2 \geq \cdots)$, the Schur function satisfies $s_\lambda(x_1, \ldots, x_n, 0, 0, \ldots) = s_\lambda(x_1, \ldots, x_n)$, the stability property defining the inverse limit $\Lambda = \varprojlim \Lambda_n$.

The Stembridge involution on the set of pairs $(T, \pm)$ of column-strict tableaux with signs gives a sign-reversing involution proving that $e_\lambda = \sum_\mu K'_{\lambda\mu} m_\mu$ with nonneg. coefficients.

The principal specialization $s_\lambda(1, q, \ldots, q^{n-1})$ equals the generating function for SSYT of shape $\lambda$ with entries in $\{0, 1, \ldots, n-1\}$ weighted by $q^{\text{sum of entries} - n(\lambda)}$.

The identity $\sum_{\lambda} s_\lambda = \prod_i \frac{1}{1 - x_i} \prod_{i < j} \frac{1}{1 - x_i x_j}$ does not hold in general; instead $\sum_{\lambda: \ell(\lambda) \leq n} s_\lambda(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \prod_{i=1}^n \frac{1}{1-x_i} \prod_{i<j} \frac{1}{1-x_ix_j}$ for the sum over all partitions with at most $n$ parts, is a consequence of the Cauchy identity.

The skew Schur function $s_{\lambda/\mu}$ factors as a product $s_\alpha \cdot s_\beta$ if and only if the skew shape $\lambda/\mu$ is a disjoint union (disconnected) of two shapes of types $\alpha$ and $\beta$.

For the staircase partition $\rho_n = (n-1, n-2, \ldots, 1, 0)$, the Schur function $s_{\rho_n}(x_1,\ldots,x_n) = \prod_{i < j}(x_i - x_j) / \prod_{i<j}(i-j)$ up to a scalar, reflecting the Vandermonde determinant structure.

For $\sigma \in S_n$ with RSK pair $(P, Q)$, transposing $\sigma$ (as a two-line array) sends $(P,Q) \mapsto (Q,P)$; in particular, $\sigma$ is an involution iff $P = Q$.
The number of paths from $\emptyset$ to $\lambda$ in Young's lattice of length $n = |\lambda|$ equals the number of standard Young tableaux of shape $\lambda$.
A semistandard Young tableau of shape $\lambda$ and content $\mu$ satisfies: rows are weakly increasing left-to-right and columns are strictly increasing top-to-bottom.

The evacuation (Sch\u00fctzenberger involution) on SYT of shape $\lambda$ is an involution $\mathrm{ev}: \mathrm{SYT}(\lambda) \to \mathrm{SYT}(\lambda)$ satisfying $\mathrm{ev}(P) = P$ when $\lambda$ is self-conjugate.
If $(P, Q)$ is the RSK pair of $\sigma \in S_n$, then the RSK pair of $\sigma^{-1}$ is $(Q, P)$, so $\sigma$ is a fixed-point-free involution iff $P = Q$ has no fixed points.
The hook-length formula counts SYT of shape $\lambda \vdash n$ as $n! / \prod_{c \in \lambda} h(c)$, and summing its square over all $\lambda \vdash n$ gives $n!$.
Jeu de taquin rectification commutes with RSK: if $w$ has insertion tableau $P$, then the rectification of any skew tableau with the same Knuth equivalence class is $P$.
The RSK correspondence is weight-preserving: if $(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_d) \in \{1,\ldots,n\}^d$ maps to $(P,Q)$, then the content of $P$ records how many times each letter appears.
Two semistandard Young tableaux are Knuth-equivalent if and only if they have the same RSK insertion tableau, giving a partition of words into equivalence classes indexed by SSYT.
The number of SSYT of shape $\lambda$ with largest entry at most $n$ is the Schur polynomial $s_\lambda(1,1,\ldots,1)$ ($n$ ones), equal to $\prod_{(i,j)\in\lambda}\frac{n+j-i}{h(i,j)}$.

The Lam-Postnikov-Pylyavskyy theory of edges in Young's lattice: the number of saturated chains from $\mu$ to $\lambda$ in Young's lattice equals the number of standard Young tableaux of skew shape $\lambda/\mu$.

Promotion on a standard Young tableau $T$ of shape $\lambda$ is defined by removing the entry 1, applying jeu de taquin to fill the resulting inner corner, and relabeling entries $2,\ldots,n$ as $1,\ldots,n-1$.

The Sch\u00fctzenberger duality theorem: evacuation of the RSK insertion tableau corresponds to reversing the permutation, i.e., if $\sigma \mapsto (P,Q)$ then $\sigma_0 \sigma \mapsto (\mathrm{ev}(P), Q)$ for $\sigma_0 = n, n-1, \ldots, 1$.
The column insertion algorithm (dual RSK) inserts a letter $x$ into a tableau by bumping the smallest entry $\geq x$ in each column successively downward.
The number of pairs $(P, Q)$ of SSYT of the same shape $\lambda$ with entries in $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ and $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ respectively equals $\prod_{(i,j) \in \lambda} \frac{m + n + j - i}{h(i,j)}$.
For a skew shape $\lambda/\mu$, jeu de taquin slides on different inner corners commute: the resulting straight-shape tableau is independent of the order in which slides are performed.
A standard Young tableau of rectangular shape $m \times n$ exists if and only if the hook-length formula gives a positive integer, which it always does; their count is $(mn)! / \prod_{(i,j)} h(i,j)$.
The RSK shape $\lambda(\sigma)$ of $\sigma \in S_n$ satisfies: the length of the longest decreasing subsequence of $\sigma$ equals the number of rows $\ell(\lambda)$ of the RSK shape.

A rim-hook (border strip) tableau of shape $\lambda$ and type $\mu$ decomposes the diagram of $\lambda$ into $\ell(\mu)$ rim hooks of sizes $\mu_1, \mu_2, \ldots$, where each rim hook is a connected skew shape with no $2\times 2$ square.

The Naruse hook-length formula: the number of SYT of skew shape $\lambda/\mu$ is $n! \sum_{D \in \mathcal{E}(\lambda/\mu)} \prod_{c \notin D} 1/h(c)$, summed over excited diagrams $D$ of $\lambda/\mu$.
Viennot's shadow construction gives a combinatorial proof of RSK: the $k$-th row length of the RSK shape equals the maximum size of a union of $k$ increasing subsequences minus $k-1$ such unions.
A standard Young tableau $T$ of shape $\lambda \vdash n$ satisfies the lattice property: for each $k$, the entries $\{1,\ldots,k\}$ occupy the cells of a valid Young diagram (partition shape).

The number of SSYT of shape $(n)$ (single row of length $n$) with entries in $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ is $\binom{m+n-1}{n}$; the number of shape $(1^n)$ (single column) with entries in $\{1,\ldots,m\}$ is $\binom{m}{n}$.
The Berenstein-Zelevinsky triangles give a combinatorial model for Littlewood-Richardson coefficients as integer points in a polyhedral cone, equivalent to counting LR tableaux.
Fomin's growth diagrams provide a local rule at each unit square of an $m \times n$ grid that encodes the entire RSK correspondence, with partition labels on vertices satisfying the four-vertex rule.
The number of standard Young tableaux of two-row shape $(a, b)$ with $a \geq b$ is $\binom{a+b}{b} - \binom{a+b}{b-1} = \frac{a-b+1}{a+1}\binom{a+b}{b}$.

The Sundaram correspondence: RSK for oscillating tableaux of length $n$ beginning and ending at $\emptyset$ gives a bijection with fixed-point-free involutions in $S_{2n}$, counted by $(2n-1)!! = 1 \cdot 3 \cdots (2n-1)$.
The plactic equivalence class of a word $w$ is uniquely determined by its RSK insertion tableau $P(w)$; the plactic monoid has a basis of SSYT under the operation of row-inserting letters.

For $\lambda$ a strict partition (all parts distinct), shifted standard Young tableaux of shifted shape $\lambda$ are counted by $n! \prod_{i < j} \frac{\lambda_i - \lambda_j}{\lambda_i + \lambda_j} / \prod_i (2\lambda_i - 1)!!$ via the Schur $Q$-function analogue of the hook-length formula.
